HEARD:

5, and 8, 2003

Madam Justice J. Mackinnon

[
1
]

A.T. lived with both of her parents until their physical separation in
February 2000.  At that time, Ms. B.T. left the family home.  She and Mr. N.T.
signed an agreement titled “Joint Custody Interim Parenting Schedule”.  This
provided for a shared parenting schedule on an alternating weekly basis up to
June 2000, but to be reviewed in April 2000.  A.T. has lived with her parents
on this basis since that time.  Ms. B.T. applied for sole custody in October
2000.  Mr. N.T. defended the application, seeking a continuation of the
status
quo
arrangement, or in the alternative, sole custody to himself.  The case
came to trial in November 2003.  In simplest form, the Court is asked to decide
whether it is in A.T.’s best interests to continue the
status quo
shared
custody or whether her best interests would be met by one parent having sole
custody.  If so, which parent?

Background Facts

[
2
]

The T.’s met in 1991.  Ms. B.T. had been married before to R.P.  The P.
marriage had broken down by spring 1985, ending in divorce in September 1987.
Their daughter, K.P., born [...], 1984 lived with Ms. B.T.  The T. began living
together in 1991, K.P. with them.  Mr. R.P. was not exercising access to K.P.
In 1993, he launched a court application for access to K.P. which was vigorously
opposed and finally settled by order made on December 18, 1994.  Mr. R.P.
agreed to not have access to K.P.  The T. marriage took place on January 19,
1996.  A.T. was born on [...], 1996.  In August 1997, Mr. N.T. was charged with
assaulting and threatening K.P.  The ensuing criminal process resulted in an
order or recognizance which prevented him from residing in the family home for
about 10 months.  During this time, he undertook individual counselling.
Counselling was also arranged for K.P. and for the couple.  All three
participants worked towards and supported Mr. N.T.’s return to the family
home.  Ultimately, this was commenced with the concurrence of the Crown’s
office, on a gradual basis.  In June 1998, the charges were withdrawn in favour
of a peace bond and Mr. N.T. did return home full time.

[
3
]

In hindsight, the family probably never recovered from the August 1997
incident and the ensuing months of separation.  In May 1999, Mr. N.T. moved
into a separate bedroom.  In November 1999, he told Ms. B.T. that she would
have to choose between him and K.P.; they could not all continue to reside
together.  She chose to leave him, found new accommodation before the year end
and moved out February 1, 2000.

[
4
]

The Interim Parenting Schedule was drawn up, signed and implemented.  At
about the same time, Ms. B.T. began dating D.B., a co-worker already known to
her.  They have lived together since April 2000.  The Interim Parenting
Schedule was never formally reviewed or extended in writing.  The parties did
both retain counsel and entered into negotiations for a final separation
agreement.  They did sign such an agreement in December 2000 which settled
their other issues, but said only this about A.T.’s custody:

17.       The parties confirm that there is no formal agreement
regarding the custody of A.T.

18.       The parties confirm that A.T. has been alternating residences
with her parents since February 1, 2000 and that this regime will continue
until a Court orders otherwise or the parties agree otherwise.

[
5
]

By the time this agreement was signed, this custody litigation had
already been commenced and defended.

[
6
]

In her application, Ms. B.T. had proposed that a custody assessment be
conducted.  Mr. N.T. was opposed to this.  A motion was brought and argued and
the assessment was ordered on April 11, 2001.  However, no assessor was named
in the order and no one had been agreed to by June 14, 2001.  On this date, the
Court heard a motion and cross-motion, one brought by each parent.  A.T. had
made statements to her Aunt, C.K., who was her caregiver at the time,
suggesting that she and her Dad were going to colour their hair, change their
names and go away.  Of course, Ms. C.K. reported this to Ms. B.T., who then
kept A.T. with her and sought interim sole custody based on fear of a planned
abduction.  Mr. N.T. brought an emergency motion to restore the
status quo
,
but nonetheless, did not see his daughter for two weeks.  The motions judge did
restore the
status quo
, made a non-removal order and required both the
parents’ passports and A.T.’s to be surrendered to counsel until further
order.  In the same order, Dr. Gerald Munt was named as the clinician to
conduct the previously ordered assessment.  The assessment commenced with the
first interview of Mr. N.T. on July 5, 2001.  The 100 page report is dated
January 12, 2003.  It recommended sole custody to the mother and access to the
father to consist of alternate weekends, Friday to Sunday evening, and in the
other weeks from Tuesday after school until Thursday morning, plus one half of
all holidays.

[
7
]

Then, on January 16, 2003, an addendum was issued by Dr. Munt in which
he amended his recommendation for access.  His amended recommendation was that
the father’s alternate weekend access extend from Friday after school to Monday
morning, that the midweek overnight access not occur and be replaced by a
weekly, Wednesday evening visit, from after school to 7:30 p.m.

[
8
]

In essence, Dr. Munt concluded that the T. could not successfully share
the parenting of A.T., that A.T. is caught in the ongoing conflict between her
parents and needs to be rescued from this “interminable hostility”.  He
concluded that the mother was the parent who could provide the greater degree
of healthy child rearing.

[
9
]

Against this recommendation stand the lengthy
status quo
and the
fact that A.T. is outwardly a happy, healthy little girl, doing well in school
and her other activities.

The Trial

[
10
]

The
evidence adduced at trial focused on a number of primary issues or events,
which also serve to identify the position of each parent.

1.

Past Parenting Experience.

•

Ms. B.T. submits that she has successfully parented K.P. but that
Mr. N.T.’s step-parenting of her reflects poorly upon his parenting abilities.

•

Mr. N.T. submits Ms. B.T.’s parenting of K.P. reflects a pattern
of excluding the father from the child’s life, inappropriate physical
discipline, and multiple, unsuccessful relationships; all of which reflect
poorly upon her parenting abilities.

2.

The History of the Shared Custody Since Date of Separation.

•

Ms. B.T. submits that the parents have struggled under the
status
quo
regime, lack the necessary level of cooperation and communication to
share custody and that this has created a situation of conflict and tension for
the child which must end.

•

Mr. N.T. submits that by and large, the parents have reached the
necessary agreements between themselves and that shared custody is working well
for A.T. and should continue.

3.

Dr. Munt’s Assessment.

•

Ms. B.T. acknowledges that the report was delayed, but submits
that it is nonetheless insightful and helpful to the Court.

•

Mr. N.T. submits that Dr. Munt’s report should attract no
weight.  In his submission, the report is inaccurate, Dr. Munt lost his neutrality
between the parents and his opinion was the result of pressure and influence
from the mother.

4.

Parenting of A.T.

•

Ms. B.T. submits that Mr. N.T. tries to undermine her
relationship with A.T. and that she is the parent who provides more consistent,
stable care for A.T. including facilitating a positive relationship with her
father.

•

Mr. N.T. submits that he is the more stable parent, that he has
not interfered in any way with the mother’s relationship with A.T., that A.T.
is flourishing under the joint arrangement and it is only for personal reasons
that Ms. B.T. opposes its continuation.

1.
Past
Parenting Issues

•

Re:  R.P.

[
11
]

Mr.
N.T. submitted that Ms. B.T. acted to exclude Mr. R.P. from K.P.’s life in a
way and/or for a purpose that reflects against her as a parent and caused him
to be concerned that her application for sole custody of A.T. is the first step
by which she may seek to curtail his role as A.T.’s father.  The suggestion was
made that Ms. B.T. excluded Mr. R.P. in favour of Mr. N.T., and might do the
same thing now, to exclude Mr. N.T. in favour of Mr. D.B.

[
12
]

Clearly,
it is not the function of this Court to try the B.P. v. R.P. case.  I have
reviewed the evidence led in connection to it from the perspective of what it
may reveal as to Ms. B.T.’s parenting capacity and credibility.  In doing so, I
have not reached the conclusion urged upon me by Mr. N.T.  The P. separated in
1985 and Mr. R.P. did not exercise access to K.P. after 1987, except for one visit
in 1988 when he appeared, unannounced, at her ballet recital.  He made one
request to see K.P. in 1989, and one just prior to issuing his application for
access in 1993.  By then, Mr. N.T. had been living with Ms. B.T. and K.P. for
some two years; K.P. and Mr. N.T. had already established a relationship.  Mr.
N.T. cannot suggest that the mother’s eloquent description of his relationship
with K.P. was overblown or exaggerated since he expressly confirmed and adopted
those portions of her affidavit in his own.

[
13
]

It
is true that Ms. B.T. was incorrect in her recollection of the outcome of the
forensic testing which had been conducted to determine whether Mr. R.P. had
paedophilic tendencies.  In her affidavit sworn January 14, 1994, she stated:

8.         As a result of the allegations made against the Applicant, a
Family Court Clinic Assessment was ordered pursuant to the Order of the
Honourable Judge K.A. Flannigan dated April 29, 1986.  The assessment was
conducted by Dr. John Dimock, then of the Family Court Clinic.  I understand
that the Applicant also underwent full sexual behaviours testing by Dr. John
Bradford of the Royal Ottawa Hospital, as part of the assessment process.

9.         I have been unable to locate a copy of the final Family Court
Clinic assessment report.  I am making arrangements to have the medical records
subpoenaed for use in these proceedings.  In any event, I recall at the time of
the assessment that Dr. Dimock and Dr. Bradford had concluded that the
Applicant had sexual paedophilic tendencies and thus, it was recommended to the
Court that he not be permitted unsupervised access to K.P.

[
14
]

In
fact, the reports were to the effect that he was an unlikely candidate for, and
that there was no clear evidence of, paedophilia.  Based on the record before
me, I am not able to determine that Ms. B.T. was, in 1994, purposefully
incorrect, i.e. intending to mislead the Court.  I do note that these reports
would have been readily available to Mr. R.P. and through him, the Court.  I
will suggest that her recollection on this issue was coloured by her personal,
negative view of Mr. R.P., which on the issue of paedophilia appears to have
been based on conjecture in 1986, but was supported in 1994 by allegations made
by Mr. R.P.’s sister that he had sexually abused her as a child.

[
15
]

Leaving
that issue aside, there was merit to her opposition to access.  She was
supported in it by Mr. R.P.’s own mother, stepfather, and sister, each of whom
filed an affidavit setting out facts and reasons why he should not have access
to K.P.  K.P. was represented by the Office of the Children’s Lawyer.  Her
lawyer also recommended that Mr. R.P. have no access to K.P. based upon K.P.’s
wishes, her lack of relationship with Mr. R.P. and the fatherly role that Mr.
N.T. had assumed in her life, by now, for a number of years.  Ultimately, Mr.
R.P. consented to a final order on December 18, 1994 that he would not have
access to K.P.

[
16
]

For
these reasons, I conclude that Ms. B.T. did not embark on a scheme to exclude Mr.
R.P. from his daughter’s life without merit or for the ulterior purpose of
inserting Mr. N.T. in his place.  Mr. R.P. had only seen K.P. some six times
between 1986-1992 and Mr. N.T. had already assumed the role of stepfather to K.P.
before the access application was launched.

[
17
]

Further,
there is no evidence of any effort by Ms. B.T. or Mr. D.B., for him to take
over the role of father to A.T.  It is true that Ms. B.T. has asked the Court
to award sole custody to her, at this trial and on her motion returnable June
14, 2001.  I accept that her fear that Mr. N.T. might abduct A.T. on that
occasion was an overreaction especially when A.T. did say that “the part about
running away was not true”.  Nonetheless, Ms. B.T. invoked the jurisdiction of
the Court and has abided by the ensuing Court order ever since, as she abided
by the agreement to share custody on an alternating weekly basis up until that
incident.  Further, by counsel’s letter dated June 8, 2001, Ms. B.T. proposed
to return to the
status quo
provided Mr. N.T. would agree to a
non-removal order, counselling for A.T. to determine why, if they were not
true, she would make such statements and daily telephone access to the child.
Accordingly, I do not equate her court application to a scheme to exclude Mr.
N.T. from A.T.’s life.

[
18
]

Finally,
it is true that Ms. B.T. had an unsuccessful marriage with Mr. R.P., followed
by an unsuccessful relationship with J.H., who abused her and whom she left.
She lived with Mr. N.T. for nine years.  She is now in a relationship with Mr.
D.B., of nearly four years duration.  There is no doubt that she had a
difficult childhood and difficulties as a young adult.  At present, she is a
mature individual with a successful, steady employment record.  Her recent
relationships are mature and committed.  Her problems from 20 years ago are not
weighty in assessing her current parenting capacity.

•

Re:  K.P. and the August 1997 Incident

[
19
]

It
is common ground that the family faced many stressors at this time, including
on the particular day in question.  They had been without hot water, K.P. had
not brought her sleeping bags in from the back yard as asked and had played her
mother and Mr. N.T. off in order to get permission to go out to a friend’s.
When she came home, she took a shower which Mr. N.T. felt jeopardized their
limited supply of hot water.

[
20
]

Mr.
N.T. admits that he shouted at her through the bathroom door, “I’m going to
fucking kill you”.  He admits that later, he went into her bedroom, spoke to
her in an “elevated” voice and when she gave him the finger, spanked her five
times on the buttocks.  He agrees that he lost his temper.

[
21
]

Ms.
B.T. and K.P. maintain that, in fact, Mr. N.T. punched K.P. with his closed fist
five times.  The next morning, the police were called and charges were laid.

[
22
]

For
the purposes of this action, on the civil standard of proof, I have concluded
that an assault did take place and that there were reasonable grounds to
support laying charges.  In my view, this was not overblown by Ms. B.T., nor
was it a manipulative attempt on her part to have Mr. N.T. removed from the
home.  Yes, it was the culmination of the build up of various factors, but no,
it was not within the scope of acceptable parental discipline.  I adopt the
description set out by the social worker, Marian Hallick, who was involved with
the family following the incident:

CLINICAL IMPRESSION:

The T. family is a “remarried or reconstituted” family in the sense that
B.T. came to the relationship from a previous marriage and had a child of 9.
From the literature we know that this type of family unit is usually faced with
a number of adjustment problems.  There are several issues and dilemmas that
challenge such a family unit.  Many of these are evident from the data
presented above.  N.T. and B.T. entered the relationship with unique
personalities and unfinished family of origin issues, including sexual abuse
and family income support problems in B.T.’s case, and a rigid family
upbringing in the case of N.T.

Couples frequently come to these relationships with relationship
fantasies that lead to unrealistic hopes and, ultimately disappointments from
having little knowledge of the kinds of personal adjustments which have to be
made particularly in the area of step-parenting.

In the T. family, the stressors were building based on inadequate
finances; the relationship with K.P.’s father and the court case; the birth of
a new baby; and, B.T.’s absence due to her work with Foreign Affairs which led
to N.T. having a lone parenting role with his step-child.  In addition, there
were time problems for the couple [sic] relationship i.e. little time to spend
alone; the additional work from moving to a “dream” home in the country;
additional travel and expenses for travel; and, the support that N.T. was
require [sic] to give his parents.  He was also under pressure at work.

It seems N.T.’ [sic] did not have the necessary coping skills to deal
with these numerous situations.  He holds a fairly rigid view of the male role
in a family.  B.T. has male role identity issues due to having had an
abandoning father and a sexually abusive step-father.  These issues impacted on
their interpersonal relations.

Developmentally K.P.’s needs were changing as she became a teenager.
This meant she was being more oppositional and outspoken and when B.T. would
take her side this upset N.T.  On the other hand, if she took N.T. [sic] side K.P.
would be angry.  The family members were unable to sort out these conflicts
appropriately.  Also, these parents had established spanking as one form of
discipline and this was an accepted pattern.  On the night of the offence N.T.
used this to excess and thankfully B.T. was able to recognize this and protect
her child.  However, in retrospect there were several indicators if the couple
had been able to recognize them which indicated that help was required to deal
with the building tensions in the house.

Based on the data, it seems that N.T. was becoming depressed and had no
outlets for his frustrations.  Against this backdrop of Axis IV stressors the
assault took place.

The family have been in counselling, K.P. has had help; and the couple
have worked on some of their issues.  In this writer’s opinion they are ready
to move on and resume living together as long as there is no major mental
illness which is not controlled.  Dr. Greenberg will assess this issue.
However, N.T. should continue with individual work and couple and family work
should also continue with a focus on the adjustment, couple communication and
step-parenting issues.

[
23
]

I
also note that Ms. B.T. participated fully in the counselling and wrote
persuasively to the Crown Attorney, all to facilitate Mr. N.T.’s return to the
family home.  In my view, she was sincere and supportive of him over these
months and this conduct is not open to criticism.  Nor do I find that Ms. B.T.
exaggerated the assault in these custody proceedings.  It was clearly
considered serious by all concerned at the time, including the participants,
the Crown Attorney, and the treating professionals.  Dr. Greenberg was the
psychiatrist to whom Mr. N.T.’s defence counsel referred him.  Dr. Greenberg
recommended in his report dated June 23, 1998:

…According to information presently available it appears that the
accumulation of stressors led to a situational threshold where Mr. N.T. lost
his temper.  He admits that his coping skills and personal resources were
stretched beyond their limits and he lashed out in a temper outburst.
Subsequently the family has sought counselling and he has attended individual
counselling with Dr. Bailey.  The likelihood of further violence within the
family is therefore dependent on Mr. N.T. utilizing and adopting the various skills
which [he] has learned from his various counselling sessions with Dr. K. Nathan
and Dr. B. Bailey.  In the writer’s opinion Mr. N.T.’s risk factors would
probably place him within a low-risk category and the probability of violent
behaviour in the short term is considered unlikely.  The writer however
recommends that Mr. N.T. continue with further counselling and aftercare with a
counsellor or therapist to monitor his mental state and coping skills with the
various stressors, some of which are still apparent in his family unit and
lifestyle.  Mr. N.T. has also been advised to look into decreasing his
stressors in the short term which are likely to reduce the risk of future
situational and emotional aggressive outbursts.  His prognosis is therefore
considered as very good at this time.

[
24
]

Reference
has been made to an accepted pattern of spanking K.P. as a form of discipline
in the T. family.  It is not denied that Ms. B.T. had spanked K.P., including
use of a belt and a wooden spoon.  There was also one occasion where she became
extremely angry with K.P. and had her hands around her neck, but either
restrained herself or removed her hands when Mr. N.T. intervened.  This is
clearly inappropriate and cannot be considered as an acceptable form of discipline
under any description.

[
25
]

In
spite of the physical incidents on the part of both Mr. N.T and Ms. B.T.
towards K.P., I am satisfied that physical discipline is not an issue or
concern with A.T.  I accept Ms. B.T.’s testimony that she made a conscious
decision not to use physical discipline after seeing fear in K.P.’s eyes.
There are a few references attributed to A.T. that one or other parent has or
may have spanked her, but, in my view, there is no cogent evidence that either
of these parents still uses physical discipline.

[
26
]

The
assault on K.P. by Mr. N.T. is a relevant consideration in assessing his
parenting capacity with regard to A.T.  The weight to be assigned to it is
reduced by the passage of time and remedial counselling taken by him since the
event.  As well, on December 16, 1997, Dr. Nathan wrote that Mr. N.T. had a
“tendency to scapegoat K.P.”.  There is no evidence of any such tendency
towards A.T.  In all, I conclude that Mr. N.T.’s step-parenting experience with
K.P., which got off to a good start, was not successful in the long run.

•

Re:  Grandparent Access

[
27
]

In
December 1994, the paternal grandparents issued an application against Ms. B.T.
seeking an order for specified access to K.P., and alleging that Ms. B.T. had
violated their previous access order.  Mr. N.T. relies on this as a
demonstration that when it suits Ms. B.T., she will cut off access, even to
people who had supported and assisted her in relation to Mr. R.P.’s access
case.  However, by February 1995, they had agreed to abandon their application
in favour of mediation which was successful in resolving the matter.

[
28
]

I do
not draw any conclusion from these events as to a propensity on Ms. B.T.’s part
to interfere with A.T.’s relationship with her father.

2.

History of Shared Parenting Since Separation in February 2000

[
29
]

The
parents agreed to a joint custody, interim parenting schedule, to be reviewed
in April 2000.  At that time, Ms. B.T. told Mr. N.T. that she did not think A.T.
was doing very well.  She identified a number of concerns.  In her view, the
transitions were difficult for A.T.  To her, the child appeared angry, bold and
argumentative on transition days.  To Ms. B.T.’s observation, household
routines were very different in the two homes, particularly as to mealtimes and
bedtimes.  She felt that she was having unwarranted difficulty in contacting A.T.
by phone at her father’s home.

[
30
]

The
parents agreed to review the situation again in June.  In May, Mr. N.T. invited
Ms. B.T. for a drive, at which time he invited her to move back home.  She says
he was sad and angry when she declined and thereafter, their communication went
downhill.  Later that month, although the schedule provided that A.T. would be
with her mother on Mother’s Day, Mr. N.T. was non-committal about living up to
this and Ms. B.T. called her lawyer.  By October, Ms. B.T. had concluded that
she and Mr. N.T. could not co-parent, primarily due to the level of distrust
that she perceived between them, scheduling difficulties and her sense that he
was undermining her relationship with A.T. She issued her application for sole
custody on October 6, 2000.  In it, she asked for an assessment into custody
and access.

[
31
]

At
some point that appears to have been between Hallowe’en and Christmas in 2000, C.K.,
the child’s aunt and caregiver, sent an e-mail to both parents.  I was
impressed by its child centered focus.  It was sent at a time when both parents
willingly accepted Ms. C.K. as A.T.’s caregiver and when her neutrality between
them was unquestioned.  This neutrality is clear in the text of the e-mail
itself.  Ms. C.K. made these observations:

She said she was confused but couldn’t tell Mommy and Daddy that.  I
first ask [sic] if someone told her she was confused or was she really that
way, she said she really was, and I believed her.  I asked if she could talk to
you two about it and she said she just couldn’t.  I asked why and she seemed
reluctant to say.  I asked if it was because she loved you both the same and
didn’t want to hurt the other and she confirmed this.  She said again she just
couldn’t tell you two how she felt.  Therefore I will.  Firstly, this is a
terrible shame that a four year old feels she bears the burden of the emotional
well-being of two adults.  What a strain for a little girl.

I asked how she felt about going back and forth every week and she said
she didn’t like it.  She told me she didn’t know where she lived anymore.  She
said I live with Mommy and then I live with Daddy, and she repeated it several
times, all the while poking herself in the head in a disturbing manner.  This I
might say is not the first time she has repeated Mommy/Daddy while poking
herself.  An obvious stress point for her.

I asked what she thought could be done about it and she said she didn’t
have a solution, that she just couldn’t make up her mind and the best thing to
do was run away from home.  HOW ABOUT THAT!

…

Please don’t ask me to take sides in this, I am only reporting what
happened.

[
32
]

A.T.
made a similar remark to Dr. Munt, noted at p. 69 of his report:

…Struggling with her weekly rotation between mom and dad’s place, A.T.
has requested an end to the burden of the repeated transitions.  When I saw
her, she told me, “I just want to stay in one place… I find it really hard
going back and forth.”  …

[
33
]

There
is an entry in the Churchill Carling Daycare log which also reflect the child’s
confusion:

March 22, 2001.  Then she said:  Well, I don’t know where to live or who
to live with, I’m confused.

[
34
]

Mr.
N.T. was of the view, at the time and today, that A.T. has adjusted well to the
joint regime.  He believes that she might prefer to live primarily with him,
but nonetheless, his primary position has always been that the joint regime
should be maintained.

[
35
]

In
support of this view, Mr. N.T. relies upon objective evidence from a variety of
sources. In February 2001, the Churchill Carling Daycare described A.T. as a
“very well behaved, mature and very sweet little girl who has potential to do
well next year in SK French Immersion”.  In April 2001, daycare personnel
described her as happy and well adjusted.  The Director of the Daycare
testified at the trial.  She stated that overall A.T. was well adjusted, happy
and outgoing.  She described her as “thriving”.  Her observation was that A.T.
appeared to be very close to her dad, and very much the same with her mother.
She described both parents as cooperative and concerned.  On occasion, A.T. did
comment that she would like to live with her father.  One such occasion is
noted under the date of March 23, 2001:

As soon as A.T. saw me [in] the a.m. [s]he said “I want to live with
daddy for ever.

[
36
]

In
Senior Kindergarten, the following year, A.T. was stated to be “a friendly,
enthusiastic, bright child who always comes to school with a big smile…A.T.
appears confident and happy…” Her most recent report card notes that she has

The Law

[
125
]

In
Kruger v. Kruger

(1979),
1979 CanLII 1663 (ON CA)
, 25 O.R. (2d) 673, the Ontario Court of Appeal set out parameters for
court ordered joint custody, at pp. 4, 6 and 8:

Whether it will be feasible in any particular case will, in my opinion,
depend on the coming to an understanding between the parties on at least two
essential matters:

(a) each of them accepts that the other is a fit parent to have custody
of the children on the shared basis to be arranged, and

(b) each of them is persuaded that he or she can co-operate with the
other, and that the other in turn can co-operate with him or her, on the basis
to be arranged.

…

Above all, it requires a willingness by both parents to work together to
ensure the success of the arrangement. Such a willingness must be sincere and
genuine; by its very nature it is not something that can be imposed by a Court
on two persons, one or both of whom may be unwilling or reluctant to accept it
in all its implications. Like marriage itself if it is to succeed, it is an
arrangement that has to be worked out by two persons who are determined, of
their own will and in good faith, to make it work.

…

…I do not see any basis on which we, at this stage in the present
proceedings, could be justified in decreeing it, in the hope, without more,
that the parties may thereby be persuaded to make it work. If we were to act on
such a hope, the result, in my view, would be a triumph of optimism over
prudence.

[
126
]

I accept that the law in
Ontario has developed since the
Kruger, supra
decision such that a court
may award joint custody even where both parents do not consent to it, if the
court is satisfied by other evidence that, nonetheless, the parties can and
will make it work.  This interpretation is apparent in the decision of
Kappler
v. Beaudoin
,
2000 CanLII 22579 (ON SC)
, [2000] O.J. No. 1558 (S.C.J.) where Rutherford J. states at
para. 17:

The cry for co-parenting is loud. I am all for it, but only where it is
likely to be better for the children than some other arrangement.  I cannot simply
turn my back, however, on the accumulated wisdom and learning in the cases and
the literature which cautions against co-parenting and joint custody in
circumstances in which the parents are unlikely to achieve a sufficient level
of co-operation.

[
127
]

In that case, there had been
a two year
status quo
with the children living week about with their
parents.  Rutherford J. took the history of this into account in coming to the
conclusion that it was not a suitable case for joint custody.  He states at
paras. 15 and 16:

…While I am inclined to favour the avoidance of unnecessary lifestyle
changes for the children, I cannot conceive that continuing the present
"stand-off" can be in their best interests. …

…In light of the evidence, however, I think such a level of co-operation
and communication to be beyond the realistic reach of the parties. …

[
128
]

Belch J. took a similar
approach in
Orth-Lashley v Lashley
,
[1999] O.J. No. 185 (S.C.J.)
.  He
quoted Professor Julien D. Payne at para. 56:

…In determining whether joint custody is a viable option, the courts
will have regard to past experience.  Where the parents have continued to share
decision making powers respecting the children by agreement or pursuant to an
interim order for joint custody following a marriage breakdown, the success or
failure of these arrangements for joint custody is a cogent factor in any final
disposition

[
129
]

It is the court’s
responsibility to determine having regard to all relevant factors, including
past experience, whether joint custody can and will work and whether, on
balance, it is the arrangement that is in the child’s best interests.  If so,
it is not also a requirement that both parents are in favour of it.  And, as
Belch J. points out in para. 61:

In determining whether joint custody is inappropriate, the court must be
vigilant that one parent's conduct, by design, is not responsible for the
failure of the joint custody arrangement.

[
130
]

Finally, in the context of
this case, the
status quo
is important because a court will not wish to
unnecessarily introduce change into a child’s life, but it is not
determinative.  Ongoing conflict, worsening conflict and lack of cooperation
have been held to be sufficient to warrant a variation of an existing
arrangement.  See
Wreggit v. Belanger
,
[2001] O.J. No. 477 (C.A.) at
para. 20
:

Conflict and lack of co-operation, whatever the source, are an
impediment to an effective joint parenting arrangement, as well as a source of
stress for the children.

[
131
]

The Court must consider the
impact of parental conflict upon the child.  Indeed, a recurrent theme in
litigated custody cases is the court’s search for the best way to reduce or
manage the conflict between the parents in an effort to promote the child’s
best interests.

Conclusion

[
132
]

Applying these principles of
law to this case, I have concluded that it is in the best interests of A.T. to
alter the
status quo
.  A.T. has done well under the alternating week
regime in most, but not all, ways.  Of greatest significant is the fact that
she is subject to the negative feelings and opinions that her father harbours
for her mother.  She has made the discomfort that this causes her known to a
variety of individuals, including her mother, her aunt, the Children's Aid
Society social worker and Dr. Munt.  This cannot be allowed to continue.

[
133
]

In my view, Mr. N.T.’s
inability to keep his own negative feelings for Ms. B.T. away from and unknown
to A.T. is the single most compelling reason against continued joint custody.  A.T.
must be permitted to grow up in an atmosphere that facilitates a positive,
enduring bond with each parent.  This is more probably achieved in the home of Ms.
B.T. than by continuing the joint custody or by Mr. N.T. assuming sole custody.

[
134
]

In my view, the level of
conflict and mistrust between the parents also renders continuing the shared
parenting inadvisable.  The parents are not cooperative with each other.  Their
communication is often acrimonious.  This has created a situation of conflict
and tension for A.T. which should be ended.  It is preferable to change the
status
quo
under which A.T. has been living, in order to reduce the level of
conflict which has prevailed.

[
135
]

As between the parents, the
mother is the more suitable sole custodial parent.  She has not interfered with
A.T.’s relationship with her father.  In addition, A.T. accepts a more
structured routine at her mother’s home and seems better able to progress
towards independence there, than with her father.  Ms. B.T. is the parent who
can be expected to better facilitate necessary parental interactions with third
parties on behalf of the child.  For all these reasons, sole custody is awarded
to Ms. B.T.
